review: This is definitely one of the greatrest games I have ever played, the replayability is incredible, Ive never had the same game twice, can't wait for rebirth.

As of writing this I am 500+ hours in and I have to say its one of the most enjoyable games I have played in a long time, It's really easy to just pick up, yet it also has the ability to make you stay playing for hours on end. Due to all the secrets, items, enemies and most importantly the difficulty it has a ton of replay value. 

When I say difficult I really do mean it but the more you play the more you learn how to overcome many of the challenges that the game has to offer.

Another reason I enjoyed it was the randomly generated levels, this also comes with random enemies, items and secrets, so no two runs end up being the same. 

The game also borrows a lot from Zelda, so if you are a fan of the level design and many of the mechanics of the early Zelda dungeons and items you will probably be a fan of this.


Other than the solid game play it is aesthetically pleasing because of Edmund McMillen's really fun and quirky art style.

I really recommend you pick up this title and the expansion pack as soon as possible.

[h1] DO NOT GET THIS GAME [/h1]

I am leaving a positive review because it's a great game; however, there is no reason to buy this game specifically.

If you've never played Isaac before, I highly recommend it. I have over 250 hours in Rebirth and counting. However, [b]GET REBIRTH[/b]. Rebirth is NOT a sequel to Isaac, it's a remake. That means it's exactly the same game but better in every way. There are more items, modes, characters, and mechanics in Rebirth, and they manage to improve on an already great game. Did I mention that they changed the art style completely? (for the better) While you're at it, get Afterbirth and Afterbirth+ too. It's more than worth the extra money you'll pay.

If you've played Rebirth and are thinking of trying vanilla Isaac (the position I was in when I bought it), I can't recommend it. It's the same game, but it feels smaller and clunkier. The game runs in Flash, so you can only get around 30FPS and it's very noticeable. All in all, it feels like, and is, a complete downgrade.

The soundtrack is 10/10, though.

What can I say about The Binding of Isaac. This is by far the best indie games of 2011 I have played. Old school NES Fans, you will not be disappointed. This game has a somewhat resemblance to The Legend of Zelda's dungeons. Even newer gamers will appreciate this addicting, simple yet complex Rogue-Shooter. Coming from the makers of Super Meat Boy, this is a sad comedic gore fest full of surprises. Note that You will die a lot at first but as you keep playing, there are a lot of things to unlock and discover. This game's price value is also a must get for your steam game collection. At 4,99€ you can't go wrong no matter what. Dungeons filled with disgusting and gory, yet funny and sad enemies, will leave you wanting more and more. I found myself a lot of times putting other games aside to go play this game. I will end this review short and simple.

For me, The Binding of Isaac was never just a game. Frankly, I don't think this game is "just a game" for anyone who plays and enjoys it...

This game is actually a depressive manifesto... The manifesto of every little child who grows up in brutal conditions, trying to forget or alter the miserable world they live in through their tears and imagination...

Therefore, do not expect to find unnecessary sentences here like "the game's graphics are like this, its gameplay is like that." This game wasn't made for graphics, optimization, or achievements... It was made to narrate the final hours of a child trapped in dark despair, helplessness, and loneliness...

The tragic part is that, even without seeing the ending on my first playthrough, I instantly understood what had happened to Isaac and why his tears were his only weapons...

It is the only game that I haven't uninstalled from my computer for years, and the one that I play repeatedly after long breaks...

For those who truly feel it...

After more than 700 hours I think it's finally time to review this game, since I think I have played a good amount to give my unbiased oppinino on The Binding of Isaac.

First and foremost: Yes, I have played Rebirth. I think it was around my 500 hour mark when Rebirth was released and I was hyped like everyone else but my interest for Rebirth died down really fast and I continued playing Classic Isaac (for a more detailed review on why I prefer Classic Isaac over Rebirth, feel free to check my Review for Rebirth.)

However, I absolutely love this game. I would even go so far and say that it's the absolute best game I have ever played and I started playing games when I had a SNES, so calling a game that was made in flash my favorite game of all time is a huge accomplishment.

The skill cap in this game is something that is insanely good, games where you can feel that you get progressively better are very rare to come across, but the more you play it, the more you learn what which items do how you can get the most out of every single floor and of course dodging, the more you play it, the better you get at it.

The cool thing is, that even after 700 hours you might not find any more secrets or anything like that, but the game never feels repetitive, since every run has a different layout of floors, the items you find are different, the bosses you find are different and the drops you find, as well.

Also what this game has over Rebirth, in my opinion, is the limited amount of Items.
Sure, there are people who say that at some point u just get specific items and just restart a run to the point where you get an item that is useful, so you limit yourself to a certain amount of items. But that's all up to oneself. You can either restart all time until you get your desired item, but you can also start off with a really bad item and get god-tier items along the way. The way how you play a run with a bad item and how you eventually make it work is all up to your skill at the long run.
What I was trying to say is, there are less items in Classic Isaac than in Rebirth, so ultimately you have more control and it is more likely that you get an item that you actually like. As I said, some might see that as a negative, since you limit yourself to certain items, but if I play 20+ runs and only get 1 run where I get 1 item that I like, that's no fun to me.

All in all The Binding of Isaac is my favorite game of all time, I would even say the benchmark for all Rogue-like games.

(Eternal Edition) As far as the eternal edition go (which is an update for Isaac that was released a couple of days ago) I totally enjoy this update. It adds a Hard Mode to the gae, so for people who have played this game for 700+ hours and don't wanna switch over to Rebirth, this is a great addition, because the name "Hard Mode" is exactly what it says.

There are "eternal forms" of regular mobs and bosses who are way tougher to beat. They have more hit points and different attacks. Another thing that they fixed, which they also added for the regular version, is the time you freeze whenever you pick up an item, trinket, pill, tarot- or playing card. The frame in which you freeze and can't move has been reduced which makes it easier for you to dodge enemies.
Once the bugs have been ironed out (there is currently a bug where you can't get out of a room when you fight the eternal form of "Loki" this update will be even more awesome than it already is.

As I said, if you love Rogue-likes, chances are that you already have this game, but if not, you should definitely give this game a try.

+ Wonderful iteration of a classic top-down dungeon crawler
+ Fantastic and engaging soundtrack; really keeps you in the game and sets the mood
+ Boasts an art-style that strikes one as being both creepy and cute
+ Hilariously strange stage-to-stage intermissions
+ Wholly satisfying variety of enemies and boss creatures
+ Tons and tons of stat-altering item pickups
+ Controls are simple, intuitive and responsive
+ Contains an additional cast of unlockable characters, each with a differing playstyle
+ No matter where you are or what items you pick up, the gameplay is entirely skill-based; this, I think, is one of the game's biggest selling points
+ Gameplay is challenging in many ways, yet the lack of pandering to the player increases the sense of reward and accomplishment on completion
+ Between the unlockables and the randomly generated playthroughs, this game has quite a bit of replay value
+ Dungeon-map is easy to use and makes navigation easy; works well to help one backtrack to items that one might have passed over in other areas
+ Multiple endings

[h1]This is not Isaac.[/h1]

Now, I know what you're saying. 'How could this not be Isaac? It says it right there, on the title!' But hold on, you're not understanding. This might be "The Binding of Isaac". This might be the predecessor to the beloved "Rebirth" remake/sequel. But this is sure as hell nothing like that game. 

I have dumped over 1k hours of my life in Rebirth, including all DLC's, that is, up to Repentance. I unlocked Dead God a year ago, at the time of writing this, and I'm currently on my second savefile. I know that game. I know what everything does; every item, every enemy, every machine and beggar; every nook and cranny. That game has virtually no secrets for me at this point. So there I was, yesterday, seeing the original flash version for sale on steam. 'Well --I thought to myself-- it's only two dollars, plus the expansion, that makes five. Might as well buy it and give it a try. It can't be that difficult.' 

One of the things that drove me the most toward Rebirth, when I started playing, was the story. I was really interested in that little Isaac kid and all the ways that the items he picked up reflected all the ways he was tortured at home. That is why it came as a surprise to me when I finally bought the game and, other than the extreme difficulty that entangles the base game --that completely goes away once you install any DLC-- the tone and overall atmosphere was very light and very much opposite to what I had expected. The pixel art aesthetic made the game look way more tame than its themes and story wanted to convince you it was. 

I kept playing. From PS4 I then went to Steam, starting from 0, but this time, with over 50 hours of experience. I easily beat Mom on my first, maybe second run. I was unstoppable. I was getting achievements left and right, and that moody atmosphere and dark story that first grabbed my attention were slowly being buried by all the knowledge that the game was forcing me to learn. I got Repentance on release date, and right away, I was looking up information about the new characters and items; on how to unlock them and what they each were. I was effectively optimizing my fun. The story was now entirely gone from my mind. I was merely looking at items, synergies, enemies. What goes with what, which one should I pick, who sould I kill first. 

Flash Isaac made me feel, for the first time, that sentiment that went away as my knowledge of Rebirth widened. This game, within the first few rooms, had made me feel vulnerable, scared and alone. None of the hours I had dumped on Rebirth would help me. For the first time in years, I couldn't even make it to the third floor without dying. This is not the same game I have spent five years playing. This is a whole different experience. Immediately I could feel that darkness upon entering the first room. Isaac is not a 16-bit little guy; Isaac is crying because Isaac is scared. Isaac is doing this because his mother is after him. Isaac is experiencing something that no one should ever have to go through. His situation is extremely unfair, and so is the game. Every room that you get yourself into will make you want to cry, because that second of Isaac's life is now become more painful than the last. After dying for the first time, I remembered an interview in which Edmund McMillen, the creator of this game, said something along the lines of 'With this game, I wanted to go all in, and fill it with all the stuff that they wouldn't let me add to Super Meat Boy'. I remembered his words about christianity, and how terrifying it was for a little kid to be scared on such a level of his omnipotent God. It suddenly made sense. All those people that seemingly prefer flash Isaac to the Far Superior Rebirth Plus DLC's. They were two different games. 

It was no help that, in my arrogance, I chose to start the game on hard mode, thinking that I would have no problem cruising through it. All those people saying 'Flash is harder', 'Flash is more unforgiving', 'In flash, it is actually difficult to get to Mom'. Oh, right? Watch me beating her on my first try.

I played 11 games on hard mode. Not only did I not beat mom a single time; I didn't even get to her floor. Eternal enemies were kicking my ass everytime I saw one, and I was finding it hard to get accustomed to the faster gameplay, and to the enemies that sometimes had more, and sometimes less health than I was used to. Everything was scary, and I was alone. 

Yes, this game is unfair, and very much so. There are a lot of room layouts in which damage is absolutely unavoidable. If Repentance's motto was 'All damage is avoidable', flash Isaac's should be exactly the contrary. And when I say this game is difficult, I mean it. People who have unlocked all achievements do not fuck around; beating hard mode with all characters is required, and that mode features something called 'eternal enemies', which are variants, recognisable for their entirely white color, that run faster, shoot larger quantities of faster projectiles, have loads and loads of health, and are, in general, and absolute pain in the ass. 

I cannot recommend this game to anyone new to the franchise. I cannot recommend this game to anyone whose enjoyement of Rebirth comes from breaking the game and ending every run having emptied the whole angel item pool. I cannot even begin to recommend this game to people who kind of liked Rebirth but wanted a more challenging experience. This one is seriously tough, and it has not aged well in any aspect. You can hear the flash engine cracking and wheezing every time you enter a new room, and in that aspect, it is very much a good thing that they decided to change the engine entirely for the remake. The people I [i]can[/i] recommend this to, though, are all the people who used to think about how the belt item makes you go faster because Isaac had to run from it, or how [strike]cricket's[/strike] max's head ups your damage because Isaac had never cried harder when they died. That, I think, is the type of people who will enjoy this sick and twisted game.

Isaac and his mother lived alone in a small house on a hill. Isaac kept to himself - drawing pictures and playing with his toys as his mom watched Christian broadcasts on the television. Life was simple and they were both happy. That was, until the day Isaac's mom heard a voice from above. "Your son has become corrupted by sin. He needs to be saved." "I will do my best to save him, my Lord," Isaac's mother replied, rushing into Isaac's room, removing all that was evil from his life. Again, the voice called to her. "Isaac's soul is still corrupt. He needs to be cut off from all that is evil in this world and confess his sins." "I will follow your instructions, Lord. I have faith in Thee," Isaac's mother replied, as she locked Isaac in his room away from the evils of the world. One last time, Isaac's mom heard the voice of God calling to her. "You've done as I've asked, but I still question your devotion to Me. To prove your faith, I will ask one more thing of you." "Yes, Lord. Anything," Isaac's mother begged. "To prove your love and devotion, I require a sacrifice. Your son, Isaac, will be this sacrifice. Go into his room and end his life, as an offering to Me to prove you love Me above all else." "Yes, Lord," she replied, grabbing a butcher's knife from the kitchen. Isaac, watching through a crack in his door, trembled in fear. Scrambling around his room to find a hiding place, he noticed a trapdoor to the basement, hidden under his rug. Without hesitation, he flung open the hatch, just as his mother burst through his door, and threw himself down into the unknown depths below.

Every room is a gamble. Every enemy a small psychological battle. Every upgrade — a double-edged sword. The controls are deceptively simple, but the depth of strategy is staggering. You’ll die a hundred times, maybe a thousand, but each death teaches something new.
What makes Isaac legendary isn’t just its challenge, but its infinite replayability. With hundreds of items, synergies, and secret endings, it’s a labyrinth of discovery that can swallow hundreds — even thousands — of hours. No two runs are ever the same, and no run ever feels wasted.
It’s brutally hard, emotionally heavy, and unforgettable.

I played this game a little just after its release then did not pick it up again for several years. Just this year I added roughly 10 hours to my playtime. I reviewed [i]Our Darker Purpose[/i] which is a game in this genre I like better. I guess it is related to the fact that it has a unique Harry Potter meets Tim Burton atmosphere.

But back to Isaac: I missed Our Darker Purpose and then I realised Isaac is a game I didn't play much. I also realised it has tons of achievements that should be unlocked. I played a lot but barely made a progress as, eventually, the game's difficulty level prevailed. 

Isaac is one of those [i]roguelike[/i] games where the dungeon you explore is always randomly generated. A new run is a new experience, always. Not just in terms of enemies but also in terms of collectibles. We have items that can be used once or an assortment of objects that can be utilised regularly and then we also have pick-ups that make us stronger. Isaac's projectiles (his tears) can change in size, speed and in other characteristics and this will be key to our survival.

But why is Isaac [i]difficult[/i]? Because entering a new room immediately has us shut inside. Until every enemy is eliminated we cannot escape (well, bombs can be used to blow the doors but they are limited). Sometimes we feel like we are confined to a small space and we have to react quickly. It should also be noted that the game uses [i]permadeath[/i]. We do not get any extra lives. Making a mistake can be the end of it. In later levels (or more like worlds) we can easily come across a new boss whose movement and projectile pattern we have to learn and this requires that we perish a couple of times.

Achievements are related to items we can find as well as game completion. The game even rewards you for completing it more than once. This gives you an idea as to how difficult Isaac is. I believe the longest run I had lasted about 15-20 minutes. The simplistic (flash-based) graphics and the religious tone (the title itself is a Biblical reference) all add to the value of the game; if you like difficult (but difficult in a challenging not annoying way) games that are easy to learn but hard to master Isaac is a great choice.

This game is simpler and smaller than the sequel Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, but it is still a great individual game. For people who have already played Rebirth, it will offer a new challenge. The Wrath of the Lamb DLC is a must, and the free Eternal Edition DLC is very difficult, on par with some of the hardest achievements of Rebirth. Unfortunately, it will also offer your CPU a new challenge, as the outdated Flash engine is not suited to such a large game.

If choosing between this game and its sequel, choose Rebirth. But both games are worth the purchase.

I think this element of the game was lost when it transitioned to a pixel artstyle and energetic OST, which somewhat dulls the horror tones in favor of a more arcade-y feeling.

I have no problem whatsoever understanding why people love this game, but unfortunately, I'm not a particular fan of arcade shooters, rogue-like elements OR permadeath, so I was never going to be its greatest champion. The most I've managed so far is killing one boss and thereby progressing to a second level, and I'm just not "hardcore" enough to get much past that, I'm afraid.

   So sure, I'm a big cry-baby who needs wimpy things like save-points to find a game truly worthwhile. But if you don't have any such failings, and don't mind an aesthetic as fresh and unique as the gameplay is retro and familiar, then you may well be one of the millions of people who swear by the genius of this product. I'm certainly a fan of Mr McMillen's sensibilities, even if I don't share his skillz in gaming.

   A word to the wise, though: apparently subsequent, slightly retitled re-releases of this game are more technically finessed, and the consensus seems to be that this ISN'T the version to buy. So you might want to look into that before forking over your hard-earned dosh (mind you, if you just wanted to give it a quick test to see if it's "you", this version on sale may well be the ticket).

   Normally I would only recommend a game like this to sickos and weirdos like my good self, but its epic sales figures suggest that the gaming world is comprised of nothing but. Who WOULDN'T love a game about a bawling baby who shoots tear-drops at bleeding-eyed monstrosities while dodging around small mountains of poop surrounded by flies? The world truly is a sad and beautiful place...

Verdict: 8/10.

The game's art style is also unique, featuring grotesque and disturbing imagery that perfectly captures the game's tone.

The game's difficulty is another aspect that sets it apart from other games in the genre. The game is challenging, with players needing to master the game's mechanics and learn enemy patterns to progress. This can be frustrating at times, but it also makes each victory feel that much more satisfying.

Overall, The Binding of Isaac is a challenging and thought-provoking game that will appeal to fans of the rogue-like genre. Its dark themes and unique art style make it a standout game, and its challenging difficulty will keep players coming back for more. If you're looking for a game that's not afraid to explore dark and twisted themes, The Binding of Isaac is definitely worth checking out.

Given the upcoming release of Binding of Issac: Rebirth, I have decided to update my review of The Binding of Issac + The Wrath of Lamb. Having doubled my playtime in the past couple of weeks i have come to the conclusion that my initial response to the game was premature.

     For those unfamiliar with Issac, the game is a Rougelike Dual Analogue Shooter. this means you controll Issac (or one of his unlocakble alternates) who fights randomly spawned monsters in a procedurely generated dungeon using his own tears as bullets. Issac is heavially inspired by retro titles, especially the original Legend of Zelda, as can be seen in the way each room is a seperate yet in many ways similar mirror of each other with some room s designated as treasure or boss rooms, and the heart based life meter.

     The presentation of Issac is that of a Newgrounds flash game on steriods. To be fair that description is fairly apt. the game is built on the flash engine and if it hadn't had the time, creativity, and vision applied to it that is what it would likely have ended up as. That flash comment is not meant in the derrogative though, the game looks and sounds beautiful (Mostly thanks to Danny Baranowsky). Because it sticks to the limitations of the engine rather than attempt more realistic graphics the game looks perfect for what it is.

     Gameplay is where Issac truly shines. The controls are simple and tight, keeping the already difficult gameplay from becoming frustrating. The best part of the gameplay though is the items. The randomly generated items ensure that no two runs are the same. These items are most awesome when they work together (Protip-Polyphimus+Technology =Awesome.). The enemies have unique attack and movement patterns that are easy to learn but will always be able to throw you for a loop.

     The only problem I have with the game is the same as it was before. The random nature of the item drops and boss spawns can make some playthroughs almost instant throwaways. This is aliviated by the sortness of the game and the rapidity of the respawn but if a few games in a row with a bad start and even I get frustrated. 

8/10. Worthy of a checkout before Rebirth comes out.

I'm giving this game a thumbs down not because it's bad, but because I just can't recommend most people waste their time on it when the far superior sequel is right there.

These rooms appear as early as the third floor, so you wouldn't have even had the opportunity to get that many items to retaliate. Nothing else really worth noting that was negative. Just think of TBOI:R with less of everything and with a lot more jank (assuming you've played it).

I would say OG TBOI is [i]maybe[/i] worth dabbling in if you've already had your fill of TBOI:R and are curious about the origins of one of the greatest roguelikes created. [b]By the way, this game only supports 8-directional movement (no analog input)[/b]. It's possible to get this game working on a Steam Deck or with a gamepad, but the movement will not feel great.

Fantastic new school version of old school games like Zelda 1 mixed with Smash TV. The gameplay is pretty simple. a 3/4ths top down shooter that allows you to shoot in 4 directions. There are also alternate power ups and bombs to use. Really simple controls like Smash TV mixed with Zelda. You are Isaac, stuck in a multi leveled dungeon. Each one of these dungeon levels is in the old Zelda 1 style where each room is 1 screen. The dungeons / basements are randomized, every room and enemy combination is randomly generating. The gameplay is fun and addictive. The only downside is no lives, no continues. There are tons of quirky weapons, enemies, power ups and bosses. Everyone should spend the $5 to play this game.

I can understand if its not for everyone, because it is an arcadey retro Zelda 1 meets Smash TV sort of game. The graphics are cute and charming, but portray horrifying things like if you were to ever see a doodle of a fetus or a doodle of someone coughing out flies and poop staining the floor. Like a sad disparagingly sort of awesome. You play as Issac who basically has to get out of randomized Zelda style dungeons. There are dozens of unique enemies with different attack styles. Few enemies seem to have predictable patterns. There are also plenty of boss battles.

The controls take some getting used to, but they are basically Smash TV controls. You use your directional pad, then you use an attack direction. So you can move right and shoot left or up, or down or right. You have a bomb button, a special findable item and an auxiliary power up button for things like pills. The main attack are bullets... which are really tears. Bombs sit, but you can push them, pills do good and bad things. Some items / power ups give you dolls for extra weapons, or a dead cat gives you 9 lives but the catch is you have 1 heart energy per life. You can also get metal hearts, that count as energy, but once they're gone you can't get them back like normal heart healths.

You play through 'basement' floor after floor marked with a boss at the end. You find keys, bomb walls, kill enemies, gamble, visit stores, danger rooms and so on. Just like Zelda 1. The only thing is that it is all randomized. The room layouts are randomized, the rooms themselves are randomized, the stores, the weapons, the items.

It is all randomized, so you'll never play the same game twice. This isn't a story based game, so it won't appeal to everyone. Its highly entertaining especially in short bursts of play. For that price, you can't miss this game.

I highly recommend the game for its gameplay, cheap price and its never the same game twice with the random dungeons.

[h1] One of the first games I ever bought on Steam [/h1]

I remember the first time I saw my cousin play this game many years ago. One look at the screen made me say: “Pffft, what a silly Zelda rip-off”, to which my cousin answered: “This is nothing like Zelda”, and he was absolutely right.
The Binding of Isaac is probably the very first Steam game I ever bought as well as the very first rogue-like game I ever played, and boy what an introduction to both Steam and Rogue-like games this was.

The Binding of Isaac was created in Flash Player, out of all places, and by none other than the legendary Edmund McMillen himself. While on the surface it may look like a Zelda Rip-off, this tiny game is incredibly deep and filled to the brim with content.

[h1] An extremely morbid story by a legendary developer [/h1]

The story is about little Isaac. He lives in a small house with his mother. He plays with his toys while his mother watches Christian programs all day. One day, his mother hears a voice that tells her that Isaac is impure and that she has to rid him off all of his impure things. Being a strong believer, she does just that and Isaac is stripped of all his clothes and belongings. A few days later the voice appears again and tells Isaac’s mother that Isaac himself is impure and needs to be sacrificed. The Mother agrees and Isaac, having heard that, finds a trap-door and descends into the unexplored depths of the basement to escape his mother. Isaac’s weapon are his tears which he shoots from his eyes like projectiles. The basement is filled with dangerous creatures and beings that want to murder poor Isaac. Such morbid stories and themes have become a sort-of-a trademark for Edmund McMillen.

[h1] Escape your mother through the basement [/h1]

Isaac is played from a bird’s eye view where you control Isaac and try to make your way through a randomly generated basement and ultimately escape his mother. You go from room to room and face whatever challenge the game throws at you. It could be a room filled with enemies, it could be room with treasure, it could be a room with a game of chance, it could be anything.

[h1] A pure rogue-like experience [/h1]

The goal is to descend as deep as you can into the basement and defeat your mother, among other things. 
Each floor normally has one room with an upgrade and one room with a boss fight. After defeating a boss, you descend deeper and do the same thing until you reach the final floor. 

[h1] So many VISIBLE upgrades and power-ups... and power-downs [/h1]

The upgrades themselves are what really made me realize how deep this game really is. The game hosts hundreds of upgrades (and more if you have the DLC) which can improve many gameplay aspects. Stronger tears, faster movement, immunity to spikes, an extra life… basically, if you can imagine it, it’s probably already in the game. Not only do they make your playthrough more unique and fun, but every single upgrade leaves a very visible mark on Isaac. If you collect a reversed cross and embrace evil demonic powers, for example, Isaac will sprout devil horns. You collected a poisonous tear which turns Isaac’s tears poisonous, Isaac will look sick. Basically, everything you collect will, in some way be shown on Isaac and in a new item doesn’t replace the old one either, but rather attaches itself as well. By the end of the game, you could be a demonic legless kid with a blonde wig and a laser eye that’s immune to bomb blasts. 

The true beauty of the upgrade system is its randomness. You really don’t know what you are going to get. You may get absolutely amazing upgrades which make you breeze through the game or you may get absolutely useless upgrades which can make your play through a lot more challenging. The randomness is what keeps you coming back over and over again.

[h1] Each time you beat the game, it gets harder and more fun [/h1]

Defeating your mother is hardly the end of the game. After you beat the game (or rather a playtrhough once) you will unlock a new floor and then another and then another and then another and… it just keeps going. Not only that, but the more you play, the more items you unlock and the better you get at playing the game, the more challenging the game becomes. It’s absolutely amazing.

Needless to say, this game can be absolutely unforgiving at times with its difficulty. Once Isaac dies (unless he has an upgrade that helps him revive) the game is over and you start again from the beginning. You can collect extra hearts and upgrades that can make your run easier but it’s never a walk in the park. After beating the game you can unlock a new character or a new item that you can use in your next playthrough. Every single run will be a challenge in one way or another. In order to unlock everything in this game, you would probably need hundreds of hundreds of playthroughs. Basically, The Binding of Isaac is a game that improves the more you play it.

[h1] A cute looking game despite its morbid nature [/h1]

The game uses incredibly simple cartoon graphics and features some truly morbid yet catchy music. Unfortunately, because of the game’s engine (flash player) the game can often get choppy when too many things are on the screen at once.

[h1] There is only one reason why I am not recommending this game [/h1]

So, why am I not giving this game a recommendation if I like it so much? One reason only. The Binding of Isaac Rebirth is out https://store.steampowered.com/app/250900/The_Binding_of_Isaac_Rebirth/.
 As much as I love this original version of the game, there is no reason to come back to this one when Rebirth is superior in every single way (apart from music, maybe). The Binding of Isaac Rebirth isn’t a sequel but rather a reimagining of the original game with the same story, an improved engine and is just a lot more fun. 

[h1] A fantastic rogue-like game but you ought to just get the superior version instead of this one [/h1]

So, don’t think this game is bad, because it really isn’t. There just isn’t much point in playing this today when a far superior version of it exists. If you are interested in perma-death roguelike games, give The Binding of Isaac Rebirth a try. This one, while still great, just isn’t as good as Rebirth.

Much like the other offerings from Edmund McMillen, The Binding of Isaac is not for the faint of heart or those who are easily discouraged, frustrated, or require a constant, guiding hand to have a good time. The Binding of Isaac will kill you, a lot, over and over, without mercy. However, the genius of its game design beckons to a bygone era where reward and punishment come purely from reflexes, understanding the game mechanics, how enemies move and fight, and a proper utilization of the tools at hand. Because of this design philosophy, Isaac will demand that you play again and again, slowly honing your skill and understanding until you no longer feel small and defenseless. The game can seem impossibly difficult upon first sitting, yet once the wisdom of time accumulates those impossible bosses will suddenly seem like easy prey compared to the horrors you now contend with on the deeper levels.

Mechanically, Isaac suffers slightly from its roots as a Flash based game, denying us some of the features and options we have come to expect even from an indie game. However, the gameplay is still brilliant enough to warrant attention and the gameplay is often spot on. Isaac catches and keeps attention with a reliance on perma-death and random pick-ups which can drastically alter how the game is played. One moment you are shooting ineffective tears at enemies, the next you are firing screen extending lasers, the next you are soaring over pits and obstructions with angelic wings. There is enough constant variety available in every play through to keep the game refreshing even on the three-hundredth run, compounded by the introduction of new bosses, deeper levels, new playable characters, and more powerful and interesting bonuses unlocked upon your continued successes.

Beyond the addictive gameplay, McMillen has crafted an art style which is often both beautiful and disturbing. The cartoony characterizations mask the devious implications of many of the enemies and items as well as softening the harsh blows presented by the sheer constant brutality of your actions. There is something about Isaac that gets into your head, a fact not discounted by the catchy, haunting music constantly calling you ever further into the abyss. It is not unreasonable to say that Isaac is not a game you can pick up over a weekend, beat, and then forget; on the contrary it will call to you in the waking world, offering one more game, one more chance to redeem all your failed attempts, one more opportunity to immerse yourself in its twisted, witty, and beautiful world.

[h1]Addictive (even if you don't like it)[/h1]

I must say: I'm not that fan of [b]The Binding of Isaac[/b], but it has a very special trait: it's addictive like hell.

Every single gameplay is a brand new one, totally different from the previous ones you had. That's because all the stages, powers and bosses you find (except for the final boss) are randomly chosen. You may have an extremely easy playing as much as you may have a God-damn-stressful one, and that's one of the reasons I don't like the game very much: I have a very bad luck.

However, either you like it or not, you'll get addicted. Even I, who swore to myself "I can't see the time to stop playing this sh*t", couldn't manage to stop before killing THAT F***ING MOTHER!!! This addiction is the game's greatest achievement.

At first glance, this game may seem simple; however, it's anything but.

You start off with simple levels and enemies, collecting items that will help (or sometimes harm) you, getting you ready to fight progressively tougher enemies. Each time you go to the next level, you are met with different enemies, and all new opportunities to get items. And just when you think you've beat the game...you haven't. I'll let you figure out what that means. 

The items, enemies, rooms, and level layouts are completely random, so you will likely never have the same exact experience in this game twice. Unlocking new characters adds to the experience, as each one has its own benefits and setbacks, making the game easier in some ways and harder in others. Because of the overwhelming amount of items and enemies, I'd always recommend playing with the wiki for the game open, just so that you never make a bad decision when it comes to picking up items. Still, some things in this game come with a learning curve and you'll just have to find out what items you like to use and which ones will make you rage.

It'll be frustrating at first, but once you unlock more items and beat your own personal records, you'll be addicted. Buying the Wrath of the Lamb DLC makes the game even tougher (so I suggest buying it after you have a good feel for the base game), but adds loads of new content, including enemies, items, levels, and more.

Honestly, I'd recommend this game to anyone I knew, even with all of the dark humor and blasphemous jokes. When you look past all of that, it's a great game with excellent replay value.
